source.title: Can LLMs Learn by Teaching for Better Reasoning? A Preliminary Study
source.authors: Xue-Fei Ning; Zifu Wang; Shi-Yao Li; Zinan Lin; Peiran Yao; Tianyu Fu; Matthew B. Blaschko; Guohao Dai; Hua-Zhong Yang; Yu Wang

page_placements.theme: Weaker or smaller verifiers and reward models improve a stronger generator through test-time selection (reranking, best-of-N)

record.tranche_reason: The study develops and evaluates learning-by-teaching methods, including using weaker students' feedback to refine a stronger teacher's prompts or training. It frames this as related to weak-to-strong generalization, but does not test fine-tuning a strong model on labels produced by a weak supervisor or measure PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper's own M2 and M3 results concern improving a teacher using student feedback, not the claim's weak-label fine-tuning intervention. M1's answer-selection and code-synthesis results do not measure improvement of the teacher model itself and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study tests learning-by-teaching: a teacher LLM is improved using feedback from student LLMs, through answer selection (M1), DPO on LbT-scored rationales (M2) and iterative ICL exemplar refinement (M3). No strong model is fine-tuned on a weaker model's labels, and no weak-supervisor ceiling or PGR is measured. The authors only frame their results as 'another attempt towards' weak-to-strong generalization (§6.2). The study does not use the original finding as a tool either, so T4/uses_without_test overstates the link; discusses/T6 fits better.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that learning-by-teaching can improve LLM answers (M1), parameters via DPO (M2) and prompts (M3). They suggest, tentatively ('might help'), that strong teachers can benefit from teaching weaker students and that diverse students help. They present this as a preliminary exploration related to weak-to-strong generalization, not a test of it.
record.recipe_differences: Uses student performance or failure feedback to score rationales, fine-tune with DPO, or iteratively revise prompts; it does not train a strong student on weak-supervisor labels or report PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: M3 outcomes vary with the student configuration and iteration; the authors report stronger prompt-refinement results with students different from the teacher in their tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: M3 compares students for a LLaMA3-70B teacher on Liar. Feedback from the weaker LLaMA3-8B student reached 66.15 F1 at T=2, versus 62.01 with the self-student; the multi-student mix reached 67.09 at T=5. Logical Fallacy gains are smaller.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Failure feedback from weaker or diverse student models can help a stronger teacher refine its own ICL exemplars, a prompt-level analogue of weak-to-strong improvement.

fits_no_version.finding: M2: DPO on LbT-scored rationales (teacher = student = LLaMA3-8B) gives 32.2 MATH accuracy, versus 30.4 for correctness-DPO.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Student-exam-based rationale scores give a more informative DPO preference signal than answer correctness alone.

fits_no_version.finding: M1 (Table 2, no rows): selecting a strong teacher's answers by weaker students' exam scores beats self-consistency. Examples: GPT-4o with GPT-4o mini students, 91.71 → 96.69; LLaMA3-70B with LLaMA3-8B students, 81.77 → 87.85.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weaker-student ICL performance can serve as an answer-selection signal for a stronger teacher at inference time.

record.problems: The M2 result is reported for one model and one test set without uncertainty estimates. M3 is limited to two binary classification tasks and one teacher model; its tables do not provide a no-feedback baseline. The paper notes that some experiments were single runs because of inference costs, and that compute-resource details were not recorded.
record.rows_left_out: M1's MATH answer-selection and LeetCode code-synthesis results are omitted because they evaluate selected answers rather than improvement of the teacher model. Other LbT analyses and error-type breakdowns are also outside the weak-label fine-tuning claim.

untested.parts: No strong student trained on weak-supervisor labels, no weak baseline vs strong ceiling, no PGR.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensemble of weak supervisors or loss variant applied to weak-label fine-tuning.
No PGR dependence on supervisor/student size, task or representations.
No test of exploiting supervisor blind spots, distribution shift, or correlated weak-strong errors in weak-supervised training.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (uses_without_test) and tranche (T4) are changed to discusses/T6. The weak-to-strong link is a framing by the authors: the 'weak' models give ICL exam feedback or failure cases, never training labels. The only fine-tuning experiment (M2) uses the same model as teacher and student. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No strong student fine-tuned on a weaker model's labels, weak-supervisor comparison, or PGR.
M2 uses student-feedback scores in DPO, but does not test the listed changes to weak-label fine-tuning or compare PGR.
The study varies teacher/student configurations and tasks in its own LbT methods, but does not measure PGR or its dependence on size, task, or representations in weak-label fine-tuning.
No evaluation of exploitability, distribution shift, or shared errors in weak-supervised fine-tuning.
No theoretical conditions or proof about a student beating its supervisor.

rows.subject: LLaMA3-8B
rows.operation_detail: DPO fine-tuning using rationale scores combining correctness and LbT scores
rows.measure: accuracy
rows.note: The table also reports Original: 29.0. Authors describe M2 as a 1.8% accuracy improvement over correctness-based DPO. This is not fine-tuning on a weak supervisor's labels.
rows.check: Teacher and student are both LLaMA3-8B (Table 4), so no weaker supervisor is involved. The row is valid only for the study's own DPO comparison (32.2 vs 30.4 correctness-DPO; original 29.0), and the result is a single run with no uncertainty.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Section 6.2 discusses Burns et al. and connects learning-by-teaching to weak-to-strong generalization, without testing or using the cataloged effect.

tranche.reason: Learning-by-teaching measures a different construct from the catalog's claim versions. It does not fine-tune a strong student on weak-supervisor labels or measure PGR.

source_check.notes: Table 2 confirms both comparisons for M1 (SUM) versus self-consistency on 181 MATH problems with 256 rationale-answer pairs. These are answer-selection gains, not PGR or evidence of the cataloged fine-tuning effect.
